c.tagline: Steel City reborn: three rivers, 400 bridges, and hilltop inclines.

taxi.fareNote: Metered street taxis exist but ride-hailing apps (Uber/Lyft) are far more common and usually cheaper for visitors.

emergency.note: 911 is the single nationwide emergency number connecting to police, fire, and ambulance.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

avoid.reason: Homewood, Northview Heights and parts of the Hill District see gun violence and offer nothing for visitors.
The South Side's East Carson Street bar strip gets rowdy late at night; keep usual awareness downtown after dark.

hood_desc: The Golden Triangle where the Allegheny and Monongahela rivers meet to form the Ohio; a compact core of skyscrapers, the Cultural District's theaters, Point State Park, and the PPG Place glass castle, walkable and central.
A former produce-warehouse district now packed with ethnic groceries, roasters, breweries, and the Saturday market crowds; Pittsburgh's foodie strip along Penn Avenue, a short walk from downtown.

A once-industrial riverside neighborhood turned hip destination, its Butler Street lined with indie boutiques, galleries, farm-to-table restaurants, and craft cocktail bars; the city's arts-and-nightlife heart.
A genteel East End neighborhood of Victorian mansions and tree-lined streets, with the upscale shops and cafes of Walnut Street; a quieter, elegant base near the universities.
The academic and cultural district home to the University of Pittsburgh's Cathedral of Learning, Carnegie Mellon, and the Carnegie Museums of Art and Natural History; busy, youthful, and museum-rich.
lodging: AC Hotels by Marriott Pittsburgh Downtown
Courtyard by Marriott Pittsburgh University Center

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink.

transit.hours: Buses and the T run roughly 5am to midnight with limited late-night routes; the historic inclines run early morning to around midnight.
transit.note: Pittsburgh Regional Transit (PRT) runs the buses, the two-line 'T' light rail (free downtown), and the century-old Duquesne and Monongahela inclines up Mount Washington for skyline views.
transit.pay: Tap a ConnectCard or a contactless bank card/phone on buses, the T, and the inclines; a single ride is $2.75. The T is free within the Downtown and North Shore zones.

transit.m: PRT 28X Airport Flyer bus to Downtown/Oakland (~40-50 min)
Taxi or rideshare to downtown (25-40 min)

tip.r: ~15-20% at sit-down restaurants is expected; round up or ~15% for taxis and bar service.

food.name: Primanti-style sandwich
food.desc: Grilled meat, provolone, vinegary slaw, tomato and a fistful of hand-cut fries stacked inside thick Italian bread - the whole lunch in one hand.

places.name: Primanti Bros.
places.note: The original 1933 stand on Penn Avenue; open late and still the benchmark.

places.name: Primanti Bros. Market Square
places.note: Central branch handy before a Pirates or Penguins game.

places.name: Fat Head's Saloon
places.note: Famous oversized headwich sandwiches and a deep house beer list.

food.name: Pierogies
food.desc: Half-moon dumplings filled with potato and cheese, sauerkraut or lekvar prune, boiled then fried in butter with onions. Pittsburgh's Polish inheritance.

places.name: Pierogies Plus
places.note: Hand-pinched pierogies made in a converted gas station since 1991.

places.name: S and D Polish Deli
places.note: Penn Avenue Polish deli selling pierogies, kielbasa and stuffed cabbage.

places.name: Cop Out Pierogies
places.note: Modern pierogi shop with creative fillings alongside the classics.

food.name: City chicken
food.desc: Cubes of pork threaded onto a skewer, breaded and fried to look like a drumstick - a Depression-era mill-town invention with no chicken in it.

places.name: Jozsa Corner
places.note: Reservation-only Hungarian house serving old Pittsburgh immigrant dishes family style.

places.name: Max's Allegheny Tavern
places.note: Century-old German tavern keeping mill-era plates and steins on the menu.

places.name: S and D Polish Deli
places.note: Central European deli counter with rotating hot lunch specials.

food.name: Fish sandwich
food.desc: A slab of battered cod hanging well over a small bun, eaten with tartar sauce. A year-round staple that becomes a citywide ritual during Lent.

places.name: Original Oyster House
places.note: Pittsburgh's oldest bar and restaurant, serving its giant fish sandwich since 1870.

places.name: Wholey's Fish Market
places.note: Landmark market since 1912 with a fry counter inside the fish hall.

places.name: Parish Lenten fish fries
places.note: Church-hall fish fries across the neighbourhoods; a genuine local institution.

food.name: Pepperoni roll
food.desc: Soft bread baked around sticks of pepperoni until the fat soaks the crumb, sometimes with provolone. Coal-country lunch pail food adopted by Pittsburgh.

places.name: Colangelo's Bakery
places.note: Penn Avenue bakery counter selling rolls, biscotti and Italian breads.

places.name: Jimmy and Nino Sunseri Co.
places.note: Family Italian grocer with hot rolls, sandwiches and imported goods.

places.name: Penn Avenue market stalls
places.note: Weekend vendors along the Strip sell pepperoni rolls fresh from the oven.

food.name: Ice cream, Klondike country
food.desc: The Klondike bar was created by Pittsburgh's Isaly's dairy in the 1920s, and the city still takes its scoop shops and dipped cones seriously.

places.name: Klavon's Ice Cream Parlor
places.note: Restored 1923 soda fountain with marble counter and original fittings.

places.name: Millie's Homemade Ice Cream
places.note: Small-batch local favourite with rotating seasonal flavours.

places.name: Page Dairy Mart
places.note: Seasonal walk-up window by the river, open since 1951.

food.name: Iron City and local craft beer
food.desc: Iron City has been brewed here since 1861 and is the mill-shift classic; the modern city drinks German-style lagers from its own breweries.

places.name: Penn Brewery
places.note: Pennsylvania's oldest craft brewery, in a historic Deutschtown brewhouse.

places.name: Church Brew Works
places.note: Brewery inside a deconsecrated Catholic church, tanks on the altar.

places.name: Original Oyster House
places.note: Iron City on tap with the fish sandwich, the way it has always been done.

food.name: Imp 'n Arn
food.desc: The local boilermaker: a shot of Imperial whiskey with an Iron City chaser. Order it at a corner bar and you will be understood immediately.

places.name: Gooski's
places.note: Legendary neighbourhood dive with cheap shots, pierogies and live bands.

places.name: Jack's Bar
places.note: Round-the-clock South Side bar, the classic late-shift shot-and-beer stop.

places.name: Squirrel Hill Cafe
places.note: Known as the Cage; unpretentious bar where regulars drink the boilermaker.

landmarks: Cathedral of Learning
This 42-story Gothic skyscraper at the University of Pittsburgh is one of the world's tallest educational buildings and a defining city icon.
Duquesne Incline
A historic cable car climbing Mount Washington offers one of the most photographed panoramic views of Pittsburgh's downtown skyline and three rivers.
Point State Park Fountain
Marking the confluence of the Allegheny, Monongahela, and Ohio rivers, this dramatic fountain anchors the classic postcard view of Pittsburgh.
PNC Park
Widely regarded as one of the most beautiful ballparks in America, its riverside setting frames a stunning view of the downtown skyline beyond the outfield.
Roberto Clemente Bridge
One of Pittsburgh's iconic golden 'Three Sisters' bridges, closed to traffic on game days and a beloved symbol of the city.
Mount Washington Overlook
The classic vantage point above the city delivers the quintessential Pittsburgh skyline photograph, especially dramatic at dusk.
Phipps Conservatory and Botanical Gardens
A stunning Victorian glasshouse filled with rotating botanical displays, its glowing glass architecture is a favorite photo subject day and night.
Carnegie Museum of Natural History
Home to legendary dinosaur fossils and grand Beaux-Arts architecture, part of the Carnegie Institute's iconic Oakland complex.
Allegheny County Courthouse
H.H. Richardson's Romanesque masterpiece of rugged stone and towers is considered one of America's finest 19th-century public buildings.
Fallingwater
Frank Lloyd Wright's masterpiece house cantilevered over a waterfall in the nearby Laurel Highlands is the region's most famous architectural icon.

train.note: There are no international trains from Pittsburgh. Two Amtrak routes call at Union Station downtown, beside the Grant Street Transportation Center: the daily Pennsylvanian east to Harrisburg, Philadelphia and New York, and the Floridian, which replaced the Capitol Limited in November 2024 and now runs Chicago-Pittsburgh-Washington DC-Orlando-Miami. Both call at awkward hours, with the Floridian passing through overnight in each direction. Rail is slower than driving here - Philadelphia takes around 7.5 hours by train - so the train is best treated as a scenic option through the Alleghenies.

bus.note: No international coaches; Toronto means changing in Buffalo or Cleveland. Greyhound (https://www.greyhound.com/), FlixBus (https://www.flixbus.com/), Megabus (https://us.megabus.com/) and Barons Bus (https://baronsbus.com/) use the Grant Street Transportation Center at 55 11th Street, next to Union Station and a five-minute walk from downtown. Typical times are about 2.5 hours to Cleveland, 4 to Columbus, 7 to Philadelphia and 8 to New York. Everything is cheapest booked online well ahead; the terminal counters keep limited hours.

ferry.note: Pittsburgh has no scheduled passenger ferry or river service to other cities. The Gateway Clipper Fleet (https://gatewayclipper.com/) runs sightseeing cruises and stadium shuttle boats between Station Square and the North Shore, which is a handy river hop on game days but not intercity transport.

half.name: Kennywood Park
half.blurb: Historic amusement park in nearby West Mifflin, founded in 1898, is known for wooden roller coasters including the Jack Rabbit and the Racer.

half.name: Ohiopyle State Park
half.blurb: Whitewater rafting hub in the Laurel Highlands, about 75 minutes southeast, centers on the Youghiogheny River's rapids and waterfalls.

half.name: Flight 93 National Memorial
half.blurb: Memorial near Shanksville, about 90 minutes east, marks the crash site of the hijacked flight brought down on September 11, 2001.

half.name: Pennsylvania Trolley Museum
half.blurb: Working trolley museum in Washington, about 45 minutes south, lets visitors ride restored streetcars once used across the region.
